newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canadian commander of Zaire force in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Canadian commander of Zaire force in Rwanda.

text.p: The Canadian commander of a proposed multinational force to aid refugees in eastern Zaire held talks with Rwandan strongman Paul Kagame on Wednesday as Uganda agreed to the use of Entebbe airport as a base for relief operations.

Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril met upon his arrival in Kigali from Uganda's Entebbe airport the 19 members of a Canadian military liasion team before a round of talks with Vice-President and Defence Minister Major-General Kagame.

The Rwandan government rejects any multinational force for Zaire as irrelevant and says it cannot use Rwandan territory for its operations following the return of an estimated 600,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees since November 15.
Uganda's foreign ministry spokesman said on Wednesday the government had agreed to the use of Entebbe airport as a base for international relief operations in the eastern Zaire crisis.

"We have previously said that they (the international community) can use Entebbe as a base for the relief efforts for the refugees in eastern Zaire and that has not changed," spokesman Louis Balinda told Reuters.
Canada, impatient with the indecision in the crisis, proposed on Tuesday that a military headquarters for relief operations be set up in Uganda.
Uganda's Balinda said a United States relief advance team had already set up base at Entebbe "and we see no problem with the Canadians joining their brothers there".
Uganda borders Zaire, but does not have easy road links with the area the refugees are in.
The Rwandan government says any international aid would best be used within Rwandan territory, providing for the Hutu returnees who fled a mainly Tutsi rebellion in eastern Zaire.
But aid agencies say a multinational force is still needed to help aid reach hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and Zaireans displaced by the fighting outside rebel-held areas.
The whereabouts of some 2,000 refugees who came out of the hills of the Masisi region into the east Zairean town of Sake on Tuesday was not clear on Wednesday.
The refugees arriving in Sake said there were many more behind them, and aid agencies believe the latest influx could herald a second wave of refugees going home to Rwanda.

Canadian Major Paul Dangerfield said after meeting Kagame Baril would brief the British and U.S. commanders in Kigali on results of talks between Western powers on the force in Stuttgart at the weekend and review the situation in Rwanda.
The Stuttgart meeting agreed on various options for the force which need to be decided on by contributing countries.
Baril stays in Kigali overnight. He was hoping to travel on Thursday to the eastern Zairean city of Goma, which is held by Rwanda-backed rebels who reject any multinational force for eastern Zaire.
But asked on his arrival whether he would go on to Goma as planned, Baril said: "Who told you that?"
Baril, 52, the commander of Canada's ground forces until he was appointed to head the multinational humanitarian relief force for Zaire, last visited Rwanda's capital last Thursday.

On Wednesday, he met Major-General Edwin Smith, the commander of a U.S. assessment team based in Rwanda, and Sergio Viera de Mello, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Great Lakes region, at Entebbe airport before flying on to Kigali.
A U.N. official, who declined to be identified, said he expected even if a multinational force was formed it would not be charged with protecting aid workers deep inside Zaire.

"In Zaire, foreign troops could help with logistics, ground support and I suppose a modicum of other services like engineering -- the sort of things that soldiers can do quite successfully -- with a degree of self-protection," he said.

"We are not talking about a multinational force deploying in an operational sense with combat troops but we might be talking about something different with a lower profile and more logistics-oriented with an airlift," the U.N. official said.
He said the Rwandan government would only be interested in having members of the force on its territory if they were here to help reintegration of returnees rather than operating in east Zaire.
The U.S. assessment team, using photographs of eastern Zaire taken from a surveillance aircraft, said last week there were only 202,000 refugees left in the area.
